title: Welcome: How This Book Works
sub: The loop, the page legend, the map, and the habits that make everything else easier
goals: Use the copy buttons, placeholder chips, practice terminal and in-page Python
Follow the learning loop: read five minutes, type five minutes, break something, fix it, build one thing
Find any chapter or command from the map of the book
Read an error message and a man page without panic
Apply the two golden rules before running any command

blocks.text: This book turns a Mac into a networking and Python lab. You will type commands in Terminal, write scripts in PyCharm, watch packets cross your own network, and finish by building a command-line toolkit that scans, resolves, probes and reports. Nothing here is meant to be only read. Every section ends in something you type, and the reading is kept short so the typing starts early.

You do not need prior experience with the shell or with Python. You do need patience with error messages, because the fastest way to learn a system is to poke it, watch it complain, and work out why. This chapter is ten minutes that save hours later: how the page behaves, how the book is organized, and the habits that keep experiments safe.
What you need

Requirement
Why

Installing tools asks for your password; the book targets Apple Silicon paths such as `/opt/homebrew`

Downloads, and `example.com` as the practice target
A Raspberry Pi, NAS, homelab server or spare laptop on the same LAN

Each chapter lists its own estimate; work in sessions of 45 to 90 minutes

blocks.text: If you do not have a second machine, `localhost` (your own Mac) works for most exercises, and the book says when it does not. Where an exercise needs a separate machine, it names the placeholder so the command updates when you set your own value.

Keep a plain text file such as `~/lab/journal.txt` and append one line per thing you learned or broke: `echo "2026-10-08 zsh does not split unquoted variables" >> ~/lab/journal.txt`. The journal turns accidents into reference material, and searching it with `grep` is itself good practice.
The loop
Every chapter is built around one cycle. Run it at a pace that suits you, but do not skip the middle steps.

items.text: **Read** one concept, no more. A section is deliberately short.
**Type** the examples instead of pasting them whenever you can. Your fingers learn syntax that your eyes only recognize, and typos teach you what error messages look like.
**Break** it: remove a quote, misspell a flag, point a command at a file that does not exist. You are looking for the shape of the failure.
**Fix** it using the message, the man page, and a guess you can test. A fix you reasoned out sticks; a fix you pasted does not.
**Build** something small that uses the idea: a one-liner, a script, a function. The projects at the end of chapters are those builds, and they accumulate into the capstone.

blocks.text: Reading a command and understanding a command are different skills. Typing forces you to notice every character: the quote that must match, the space that must exist, the flag that comes before the argument. Recognition is what you get from reading; recall is what you need at a prompt, and recall comes from production.

blocks.text: Progress, ticked project steps, exercise answers and your placeholder values are stored in your browser, so they survive a reload. The search box at the top finds commands and topics (press `/` to jump to it), the **Atlas** lists every command card in the book, and the **Practice** hub gathers every exercise.
Copy buttons and the `$` convention
A transcript like this one shows a command and then its output:

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ head -3 users.csv
name,role,ip,port
alice,admin,10.0.0.5,22
bob,dev,10.0.0.12,8080

blocks.text: You type `cd ~/lab` and `head -3 users.csv`. The `$` stands for your shell prompt and is never part of the command. The output above was produced by the simulator that powers the practice terminal, so it matches what the lab files give you on your own Mac. Blocks labelled *sample output* come from a real machine of the kind you use, but the addresses and numbers will differ from yours.

When you paste several lines into zsh, a trailing comment such as `ls  # list files` fails with `ls: #: No such file or directory` (and the same for `list` and `files`), because zsh does not treat `#` as a comment character in an *interactive* session unless you ask it to (`setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS`), so the words are passed to `ls` as arguments. A line that *starts* with `#` gives `zsh: command not found: #`. The copyable blocks in this book avoid trailing comments for that reason. Script files, which you create with the `file` blocks, can contain comments freely.
Placeholders and My Values
Commands that need *your* data use a placeholder. Click the chip and type a value, and every occurrence in the book changes:

Some values are best found by asking your Mac (your IP address, your gateway, your interface name). The **My Values** tool below fills them in for you from the output of a short command. You will meet it again in [Setting up your lab](#setup) and in [See your own network](#net-local). Skim it now, and come back after setup.
Python in the page

Python examples marked with a **Run** button execute right here. They cannot open network sockets or read your real files, which is why the networking programs later in the book run in your own Terminal and PyCharm instead. For everything else the in-page runner is the quickest way to test an idea.
Change `word` to something else and press Run. Nothing you do in the page can break anything.
Anatomy blocks
When a command has several parts, an anatomy block names each part. Tokens are joined into one command line in the same order you would type them:

tokens.exp: an option (also called a flag): stop after three probes
an argument: the thing the program works on

blocks.text: Almost every command you will type has this shape: a **program name**, then **options** that change its behavior, then **arguments** that say what to act on. Chapter [zsh basics](#zsh-basics) takes that apart properly.

blocks.text: Running threads connect the chapters. The **shell tools** (`netcheck.zsh`, `lan-inventory`, `dnscheck`, `latency-log`) grow chapter by chapter in the zsh and network parts. The **Python tools** (`ipcalc.py`, `loganalyzer.py`, `portscan.py`) grow in the Python part. The first capstone merges both lines into `netkit`. The **web thread** builds a device dashboard: pages and styles, then JavaScript against the book's practice server, then a Node.js API, and the second capstone joins them into a working app on your LAN.

The minimum path to useful skills is Welcome, Setup, [Streams, redirection and pipes](#pipes), the [Text-processing toolkit](#text), [See your own network](#net-local), and [Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot). Everything else deepens those.
Learning from errors

Most of your time at a prompt will be spent reading messages that begin with a program name and end with a complaint. Treat them as information, not as verdicts. A well-formed error has three parts: **who** complained, **what** it tried to do, and **why** it failed.

blocks.code:
ls: /nonexistent: No such file or directory
│   │            └─ why: the kernel says the path does not exist
│   └─ what: the path it was asked to list
└─ who: the program that is reporting

blocks.text: Read the message once, slowly, before doing anything. Then use this method:

items.text: **Read the last line first** for programs that print long reports. Python tracebacks, for example, put the actual error at the bottom and the call chain above it.
**Check the obvious**: typos, quotes, current directory (`pwd`), spelling of the file name (`ls`).
**Change one thing at a time** and run again. Two simultaneous changes tell you nothing about which one mattered.
**Search the exact text** of the message, minus the parts that are yours (paths, host names). The words after the program name are what other people searched for.
**Check the exit status** with `echo $?` when a command prints nothing and you still suspect it failed. Zero means success; anything else means failure. The next chapters explain why.

blocks.text: These are the messages you will meet in the first week:

head: Message
What it means
First thing to try
rows: zsh searched every folder in `PATH` and found no program called `foo`
Check spelling; `echo $PATH`; is the tool installed (see [Setting up your lab](#setup))?
The path you gave does not exist from where you are standing
`pwd` and `ls` to see where you are; check the spelling and the case
The file exists but your user may not read, write or execute it
`ls -l` to read the permission bits (chapter [Files and permissions](#files))
A macOS protection (SIP or a privacy permission) blocked the action, even for `sudo`
Check Terminal's access under System Settings > Privacy & Security
zsh tried to expand a wildcard, nothing matched, and zsh treats that as an error
Quote the pattern if you want it passed literally: `'*.xyz'`
`usage: ...` after a complaint about an option
BSD tools on macOS print their usage line when you give an unknown flag
The machine answered, and nothing is listening on that port
Is the service running? Is the port number right?
DNS could not turn the name into an address
Try an IP address to separate DNS problems from connectivity problems

blocks.text: In Terminal, run `ls /nonexistent`, then `lss`, then `ls -z`. For each one, say who complained, what it tried to do, and why it failed. You will need these skills in every chapter.
Reading a man page

Every standard command ships with a manual page. It is the authoritative description of what the command does on *your* system, which matters on macOS because its tools come from BSD and differ from the GNU versions that most online examples assume. Open a page with `man`:
The page opens in a pager (`less`), so you navigate it with these keys:

head: Key
Action
rows: Jump to the top / to the bottom
Quit and return to the prompt

blocks.text: A page is organized into fixed sections. The two you will use most are **SYNOPSIS** (the shape of a valid command line) and **DESCRIPTION** (every flag, in BSD pages). **EXAMPLES**, **EXIT STATUS** and **SEE ALSO** are worth a glance. Read the synopsis as a grammar:

blocks.title: Reading a SYNOPSIS line (from man head)

tokens.exp: optional (square brackets); the bar means "choose one": either lines or bytes
optional; the dots mean "one or more of these may follow"

blocks.text: The conventions: anything in `[ ]` is optional, `|` separates alternatives, `...` means repeatable, and plain words stand for a value you supply. The same rules decode the usage lines BSD tools print when you misuse them.
Pages live in numbered sections, and the same word can appear in several. The number goes before the name:

blocks.name: man (first look)
blocks.sum: Display the manual page for a command, file format or system call.

how.text: `man` finds the page in the directories listed in `MANPATH`, formats it with `mandoc` and hands the result to a pager, normally `less`. Search inside the pager with `/`. With `-k` it searches the one-line descriptions of every installed page instead, which is how you discover a command when you only know the topic.
The formatted text uses backspace overstrikes for bold and underline. If you pipe it anywhere, pass it through `col -b` first to strip them.

flags.d: Search page names and descriptions for the keyword (same as `apropos`).
Print the one-line description of the page (same as `whatis`).
Show every matching page, one after another, instead of only the first.

examples.desc: Read the page for head and quit with q
Open the file-format page instead of a command page
Print only the lines of the ls page that mention modification time
Count how many pages mention the word packet in their description

gotchas: Piping `man` output without `col -b` leaves invisible overstrike characters that break `grep` and `awk` matches.
notes: BSD tools often reject `--help`, but the complaint they print includes a `usage:` line, which is a faster summary than the full page.

blocks.title: macOS pages differ from Linux pages

blocks.text: Search results from the web usually assume GNU tools, whose man pages describe flags that macOS does not have (`sed -i` without an argument, `grep -P`, `ls --color`, `readlink -f`). Always confirm a flag in `man` on your own Mac. When the book knows of a difference, it says so in a callout like this one.
Two golden rules
Experimenting is the point of the book, so the safety rules are short and concrete.
Rule 1: never run what you do not understand

Before you press Return on anything copied from the web, a chat, or this book, be able to say what each part does. If you cannot, look the unknown part up with `man` or the card in the [Atlas](#atlas). Two techniques make this cheap:

items.text: **Put `echo` in front.** The shell expands wildcards, variables and `$( )` before the command runs, so `echo` shows you the exact arguments the real command would receive. `echo rm *.log` lists the files that `rm *.log` would delete, and removes nothing.

**Read downloaded scripts before running them.** Piping a download straight into a shell (`curl ... | sh`) runs code you have not seen. You will do it once, for the Homebrew installer, after reading why that one is acceptable. For anything else, download first, read the file, then run it.

blocks.text: That `echo` ran nothing. It showed you that the shell turned the pattern `/etc/ho*` into a single argument, `/etc/hosts`, before `rm` was ever involved.

`rm -rf` (deletes without asking), `dd` (writes raw bytes to a device), `diskutil erase...`, `sudo` anything, `chmod -R`, `mv` onto an existing file and `>` into an existing file (both overwrite silently). None of these appear in this book without a warning and a safer way to try them. Practice destructive commands only on files inside `~/lab`, which you can recreate in seconds with the Lab Kit.
Rule 2: start with read-only commands

Look before you touch. Programs that only *display* information cannot damage anything, and a surprising amount of networking work is looking: reading an address, a routing table, a DNS answer, a log. Work in this order:

head: Stage
Examples
Risk
rows: Real: back up or use `~/lab` first
High: read the page, then run

blocks.text: When something does go wrong, press [[⌃C]] to interrupt a running command, and remember that the lab folder is disposable. If you destroy it, the Lab Kit rebuilds it. Anything outside `~/lab` should be covered by Time Machine or another backup before you experiment with commands from the "Change" row.

Later chapters scan ports, capture packets and test connections. Do that only on your own Mac, your own LAN, `localhost`, a lab machine you control, and `scanme.nmap.org` (which the Nmap project explicitly allows for light testing). Scanning other people's systems without permission can be illegal and is always rude. The book repeats this wherever it matters.
Practice
The exercises below use only Terminal and the browser. Open Terminal now (press [[⌘Space]], type `Terminal`, press Return); [Setting up your lab](#setup) shows how to configure it properly.

blocks.title: Meet the prompt

task.text: In Terminal, run these four commands one after another and write down, for each, what kind of information it prints: `echo hello`, `echo $SHELL`, `whoami`, `date`. Then run `echo $SHELL` again and read the result: it should name the program that is interpreting what you type.

hints: Each command prints one line. `$SHELL` is a variable; the shell replaces it with its value before `echo` runs.

why.text: `echo` prints its arguments. `$SHELL` is replaced by the path of your login shell (normally `/bin/zsh` on a modern Mac), `whoami` prints your account name and `date` prints the system clock. The shell does the substitution, which is the first example of a theme you will see constantly: the shell rewrites your line, then runs the command with the rewritten arguments.

blocks.verify: [[ $SHELL == */zsh ]] && echo "OK: your login shell is zsh"

blocks.title: Provoke and read errors

task.text: Run each of these, then explain in one sentence who complained, what it was trying to do, and why it failed. Fix each so it succeeds.

items.text: `cat`  (it waits for input; press [[⌃D]] to end it)

hints: For `lss`, ask yourself whether the shell or a program is reporting the problem.
For `ls -z`, read the line that begins with `usage:` and compare the flag you gave to the list in brackets.
blocks.solution:
ls /nonexistent
ls /
lss
ls
ls -z
ls -l
cat

why.text: The first is reported by `ls`, which asked the kernel for a path that does not exist. The second is reported by zsh itself, which found no program called `lss` in `PATH`. The third is `ls` rejecting a flag it does not know and printing its usage line. The fourth is no error at all: `cat` with no file argument reads stdin, so it sits waiting for you, and [[⌃D]] sends end-of-input. Knowing *which program* is speaking tells you where to look.

blocks.title: Dry run with echo

task.text: Without deleting anything, show the exact list of files that the command `rm /etc/p*` would receive as arguments. Then run `echo /etc/p*` and count the results by piping into `wc -w`.

hints: Put one word in front of the command you are unsure about.

why.text: The shell expands `/etc/p*` into a list of matching paths before running anything. `echo` prints that list instead of acting on it, and `wc -w` counts the words. Use `echo` as a preview whenever a wildcard sits next to a destructive command.

blocks.title: Find a flag in a man page

task.text: Using only `man ls` (no web search), find the flag that sorts a long listing by modification time, newest first, and the flag that prints sizes in human-readable units (K, M, G). Then run a command that uses both and shows your home folder.

hints: Open the page, press `/` and type the word you are looking for, then `n` for the next match.

why.text: `-t` sorts by modification time (newest first), `-h` makes sizes human-readable when combined with `-l`, and `-l` selects the long format. Flags can be merged into one cluster (`-lth`) because each is a single letter. You found them by searching the page, which is the skill that transfers to every other command.

blocks.title: Which of these cannot hurt?

task.text: Sort these commands into "read-only" and "changes something": `ls -l`, `cat access.log`, `sort access.log > access.log`, `ping -c 1 192.168.1.1`, `mv notes.txt old.txt`, `dig example.com`, `echo hi >> log.txt`, `head -3 users.csv`.

hints: Look for redirection operators and for commands that create, move or remove.
blocks.solution:
Read-only: ls -l, cat access.log, ping -c 1 192.168.1.1, dig example.com, head -3 users.csv
Changes something: sort access.log > access.log (empties the file), mv notes.txt old.txt (renames), echo hi >> log.txt (appends to a file)

why.text: A redirection operator turns a harmless command into a file write: `sort access.log > access.log` truncates the file before `sort` reads it, which destroys the data. `ping` and `dig` send packets but change nothing on your Mac. Always read the whole line, including what comes after the command.

blocks.title: Run a checked Python exercise

task.text: This is how Python exercises work: write code in the box, press the check button, and read the message if an assertion fails. Make the program print exactly `Hello, network!` on one line.

why.text: The page runs your code and gives the checker the text your program printed in a variable named `out`. The checker compares it with the expected text and shows its message when the comparison fails. Later exercises check return values of functions the same way.

blocks.check: assert out.strip() == "Hello, network!", "Print exactly: Hello, network!"

questions.q: What should you do after you deliberately break something in the learning loop?

options.text: Read the error, form a guess, and fix it
Paste the first fix you find online

questions.why: Fixing a failure you caused, using the message and the manual, is where recall is built. A pasted fix teaches you nothing about why it worked.

questions.q: In a transcript block, a line begins with `$ `. What do you type?

options.text: Only the text after the dollar sign and space
The text after the dollar sign, followed by `exit`

questions.why: The `$` stands for your prompt. It is not part of the command.

questions.q: Which key quits a man page?
questions.why: `man` shows pages through `less`, and `q` quits it.

options.text: Deletes nothing and prints an error
Prints the command with the wildcard expanded, deleting nothing

questions.why: The shell expands the wildcard, then `echo` simply prints the resulting arguments. It is a free preview of what `rm *.log` would receive.

questions.q: In a SYNOPSIS line, what does `[-n count | -c bytes]` mean?

options.text: Optionally give `-n` with a count, or `-c` with a byte count, but not both
`count` and `bytes` are literal words you must type

questions.why: Square brackets mark optional parts, the bar separates alternatives, and plain words stand for values you supply.
Listing a directory changes nothing. The others truncate, rename or append to a file.

A value a command acts on, such as a file name or a host name
The manual entry for a command, opened with `man`
A yellow chip in the book that stands for a value you choose, such as a host name
The number a finished program returns to the shell: zero for success, non-zero for failure
